title_options: Could A T. rex Outrun Your Car?
facts: Sellers et al. 2017, PeerJ 5:e3420 (doi 10.7717/peerj.3420): a multibody computer model of T. rex with skeletal stress analysis; running gaits gave unacceptably high bone loads, limiting it to walking; top speed about 20 km/h (5.6 m/s).
Hutchinson & Garcia 2002, Nature 415:1018: fast running would need an implausibly large share of body mass as leg extensor muscle (reported as 43% per leg / 86% total at ~20 m/s).
Mass about 8 tonnes for large adults (e.g. FMNH PR 2081 'Sue', estimates ~8.4 t).

scenes.narration: The real T. rex probably couldn't run. Not even a jog.
It weighed about eight tonnes. That's six cars, balanced on two legs.
Scientists rebuilt it in a computer, bone by bone and muscle by muscle, then asked it to sprint.
At every running speed, its leg bones took so much force they would likely have broken.
A fast runner that size needs more than forty percent of its body in leg muscle. T. rex had nowhere near that.
So its top speed was a fast walk. About twenty kilometres an hour.
A car on a city road, at fifty, leaves it behind in seconds.
So how did a giant that couldn't run catch anything at all?
